items.passage: Teeth, claws, and other animal “tools” are often reinforced through biomineralization: vertebrate teeth, for instance, contain calcium-based crystals embedded in an organic matrix. Such crystals, however, limit how sharp an edge can be. Examining the mandibles of leaf-cutter ants (Atta cephalotes), biologist Robert Schofield and colleagues found that the zinc hardening their mandibles is spread uniformly through the protein, likely bound as individual atoms rather than concentrated in separate mineral particles. The team hypothesizes that this uniformity permits a finer, more durable edge, greatly reducing the force the ants need to cut.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
options: It summarizes research suggesting that an insect’s mouthparts are reinforced in the same way as vertebrate teeth but with a different element, which may allow a sharper edge.
It describes a study that used an insect’s mouthparts as a point of comparison in order to determine whether vertebrate teeth are weakened by the minerals they contain.
It summarizes research suggesting that an insect’s mouthparts are strengthened in a way that departs from a common approach and may make cutting easier.
It describes a study showing that leaf-cutter ants need less force to cut leaves than other insects do because their mandibles contain an unusually large amount of zinc.
items.explanation: The first two sentences describe a common approach: animal tools are often strengthened with mineral crystals, which limit sharpness. The text then reports that leaf-cutter ant mandibles are strengthened differently, with zinc spread evenly as single atoms rather than as mineral particles, and that the researchers think this lets the ants cut with much less force. Choice C names both parts: a departure from the usual way of strengthening tools, and the likely benefit for cutting.

A.recipe: first clause partly true, later clause contradicted (REV)
A.why_wrong: The mandibles are reinforced with a different element (zinc rather than calcium), but not in the same way: vertebrate teeth contain crystals, while the zinc in the mandibles is spread evenly through the protein rather than concentrated in mineral particles. That difference is the point of the text.

B.why_wrong: The minerals in vertebrate teeth are background in the text, not what the study set out to test. The researchers examined the ants’ own mandibles, and nothing is said about vertebrate teeth being weakened.

D.recipe: first clause true, invented comparison and wrong cause (INV)
D.why_wrong: The text does say the ants may need much less force to cut, but it credits the even spread of the zinc, not its amount, and it never compares the ants with other insects. It also presents the benefit as a hypothesis, not as something the study showed.

sources.what: Schofield et al. (2021, Scientific Reports): Zn distributed homogeneously, likely as individual atoms, in ant (Atta cephalotes) mandibular teeth; homogeneity enables sharper tools than materials with biomineral inclusions; hypothesized large force reduction

items.notes: Area: natural science (biomaterials). Key C. Key parts: 2 (strengthened in a way that departs from a common approach; may make cutting easier). Section 6 checks: key 24 words; options 22 to 27 words; distractors with a true first clause and a false later clause: A and D (2 of 3; both rewritten in review). The force estimate (about two thirds lower than for plain materials in the paper; press reports compare with human-tooth materials) is given only as 'greatly reducing'.

items.passage: To estimate the intensity of geomagnetic storms that predate modern instruments, researchers often rely on historical descriptions of auroras. Studying a red aurora seen over Kyoto, Japan, on September 17, 1770, polar scientist Ryuho Kataoka and literature scholar Kiyomi Iwahashi paired a painting of the event in the manuscript Seikai with a newly discovered diary that described the glow’s position relative to the Milky Way. Reconstructing the aurora’s geometry from these sources, they concluded that the storm was comparable to, or slightly larger than, the 1859 Carrington event, the greatest magnetic storm of the past two centuries.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
options: It discusses a study that combined an artwork and a written account to help gauge the intensity of an event that occurred too early to be measured directly.
It discusses a study that compared an artwork with a written account to determine which offers the more reliable description of a historical aurora.
It discusses a study that drew on an artwork and a written account mainly to establish where in the sky over Kyoto a historical aurora appeared.
It describes how two historical sources were used to establish that the 1770 storm was the most intense magnetic storm ever recorded.
items.explanation: The first sentence explains that the strength of storms older than modern instruments must be estimated from historical accounts of auroras. The text then describes how two researchers used a painting and a diary together to reconstruct the 1770 aurora and judge how strong that storm was. Choice A states this purpose: the study joined an artwork and a written account to gauge an event that occurred too early to be measured directly.

B.why_wrong: The researchers did use a painting and a diary, but they used them together; the text never says they set out to judge which source was more reliable.

C.recipe: partial: a step in the method offered as the aim (PART)
C.why_wrong: The researchers did reconstruct the aurora’s position and shape, but only as a means: the text opens with the problem of estimating the strength of old storms and ends with their conclusion about this storm’s strength, so locating the aurora was not the study’s main aim.

D.recipe: first clause true, overreach on a hedged finding (BROAD)
D.why_wrong: The researchers did use two historical sources together, but they concluded only that the 1770 storm was comparable to, or slightly larger than, the Carrington event; the text does not say it was established as the most intense storm ever recorded.

sources.what: Kataoka and Iwahashi (2017, Space Weather): Seikai painting and newly discovered Kyoto diary (aurora position relative to the Milky Way) used to reconstruct the 17 September 1770 aurora; storm comparable with or slightly larger than the September 1859 storm

items.notes: Area: natural science (space physics, with history). Key A. Key parts: 2 (combined an artwork and a written account; to gauge an event that predates direct measurement). Section 6 checks: key 24 words; options 24 to 27 words; distractors with a true first clause and a false later clause: B, C and D (3 of 3). C rewritten in review (was a frequency comparison, off-text).
band7_moves: dual purpose: method (two kinds of historical source used together) and aim (gauging a storm older than instruments)

B keeps the two sources and changes the aim (which is more reliable); C keeps the two sources and offers a real step of the method (locating the aurora) as the aim; D keeps the method and overreaches the hedged conclusion ('comparable to, or slightly larger than') into 'most intense ever recorded'

items.passage:
The following text is from Archibald Lampman’s 1895 poem “The Poet’s Possession.” The speaker addresses a farmer.

Think not, oh master of the well-tilled field,
This earth is only thine; for after thee,
When all is sown and gathered and put by,
Comes the grave poet with creative eye,
And from these silent acres and clean plots,
Bids with his wand the fancied after-yield,
A second tilth and second harvest, be,
The crop of images and curious thoughts.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
options: To argue that a poet has a stronger claim than a farmer to the land the farmer has cultivated
To suggest that writing poetry, like farming, requires patient effort over the course of a season
To describe how a poet helps a farmer bring in a second harvest after the first has been gathered
To assert that a farmer’s land can also serve as a source of imaginative work for a poet
items.explanation: The speaker tells the farmer not to think the land belongs only to him. After the harvest, a poet comes and draws from the same “silent acres” a different kind of crop: “images and curious thoughts.” The poem therefore asserts that the farmer’s land also feeds a poet’s imagination, as choice D says.

A.why_wrong: The speaker says the earth is not “only” the farmer’s, so the poet shares in it; the poem never ranks the two claims, and the poet’s harvest comes “after” the farmer’s, not in place of it.

B.why_wrong: The poem sets the poet’s work after the farmer’s, but it never says that writing poetry takes patient effort or compares the labor involved in the two.

C.why_wrong: The “second harvest” is a figure for the images and thoughts the poet draws from the land; the poet does not help the farmer gather any actual crop.

sources.what: Lampman, Lyrics of Earth (Boston: Copeland and Day, 1895), poem “The Poet’s Possession”, text copied exactly

items.notes: Literature (poem). Key D. Hard band 6: the key needs two linked steps (the addressee is the farmer; the 'second harvest' is the poet's imaginative crop) and is paraphrased away from the poem's words. Each wrong option uses a real element of the poem (A overreaches 'not only thine' into a stronger claim for the poet; B the poet coming after the harvest; C a literal 'second harvest'). Context line added (the speaker addresses a farmer), as CB adds situation lines.

fixes: replaced A (praise for the farmer) with an overreach on “not only thine” (a poet’s stronger claim to the land)

band7.why: Planned band 6. Archaic diction and a figurative “second harvest” the key paraphrases away; A (overreach on “not only thine”) and C (literal second harvest) are close traps.

items.passage: Kazi Nazrul Islam (1899–1976), now honored as the national poet of Bangladesh, was raised in a Muslim family in Bengal and is credited with introducing Islamic devotional songs into mainstream Bengali popular music. <u>He also wrote more than 500 Hindu devotional songs, including Shyama Sangeet, hymns addressed to the goddess Kali.</u> Some Muslim critics consequently denounced him as an unbeliever. Yet compositions from both traditions remain widely performed, and Nazrul is frequently celebrated as a champion of communal harmony between Bengal’s Hindus and Muslims.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
options: It describes a body of songs that Nazrul turned to after critics objected to his Islamic music, illustrating how he responded to that criticism.
It identifies a part of Nazrul’s work that drew hostility from some fellow Muslims and that helps account for the way he is celebrated today.
It introduces the songs for which Nazrul is best known in Bangladesh, which the text suggests explains why he was named the country’s national poet.
It points to songs that led some Muslim critics to denounce Nazrul and that, according to the text, are now seldom performed.
items.explanation: The underlined sentence reports that Nazrul, raised a Muslim, also wrote hundreds of Hindu devotional songs. The next sentence says some Muslim critics denounced him for these songs, and the last sentence says that, because songs from both traditions are still performed, he is celebrated as a champion of Hindu-Muslim harmony. So the sentence identifies work that provoked hostility and that helps explain his reputation, as choice B says.

A.recipe: first clause true, invented sequence and cause (INV)
A.why_wrong: The sentence does describe a body of Nazrul’s songs, but the text never says he turned to them after criticism; the critics objected to these Hindu songs, not to his Islamic music.

C.recipe: first clause true, invented reputation and cause (INV)
C.why_wrong: The text does not say these are his best-known songs, and it gives no reason for his title of national poet.

D.recipe: first clause true, later clause reversed (REV)
D.why_wrong: The songs did lead some Muslim critics to denounce Nazrul, but the last sentence says compositions from both traditions remain widely performed, not that the Hindu songs have fallen out of use.

sources.what: Nazrul brought Islamic devotional songs into mainstream Bengali music; wrote over 500 Hindu devotional songs; some Muslims criticised him for writing Shyama Sangeet and declared him kafir; national poet of Bangladesh

items.notes: Area: humanities (music, literature). Key B. Key parts: 2 (drew hostility from some fellow Muslims; helps account for how he is celebrated). items.passage: Amborella trichopoda, a shrub with small, creamy white flowers, grows wild only on Grande Terre, the main island of New Caledonia in the southwest Pacific. Phylogenetic analyses consistently identify the species as the sister group to all other extant flowering plants: its lineage diverged from theirs more than 130 million years ago, and it is that lineage’s only surviving member. By comparing Amborella with other flowering plants—its wood, for instance, lacks the water-conducting vessel elements that most angiosperms possess—botanists can reconstruct characteristics the earliest flowering plants probably shared.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
options: To introduce a plant species and explain why its place in evolutionary history makes it useful to scientists studying early flowering plants
To introduce a plant species and argue that the earliest flowering plants must have closely resembled it, since it has changed little in 130 million years
To introduce a plant species and explain how botanists have used its wood to determine when flowering plants first appeared
To introduce a plant species and suggest that its isolation on a single island explains why its lineage has survived for so long
items.explanation: The text introduces Amborella trichopoda and where it grows, then explains that its lineage split from all other living flowering plants more than 130 million years ago. Because of that position, comparing it with other flowering plants helps botanists infer the traits of the earliest flowering plants. Choice A states this purpose.

B.recipe: first clause true, overreach on the inference (BROAD)
B.why_wrong: The text says comparisons with Amborella help botanists infer what early flowering plants probably shared; it never says the earliest flowering plants must have looked like it or that the species has changed little.

C.recipe: first clause true, invented use of a detail (INV)
C.why_wrong: The wood is one trait compared with other flowering plants to infer early characteristics; the 130-million-year figure comes from the species’ lineage, and the text never says the wood was used to date anything.

D.why_wrong: The text says the shrub grows wild only on Grande Terre and that its lineage is very old, but it never links the two or explains why the lineage survived.

sources.what: Amborella trichopoda: endemic to Grande Terre, New Caledonia; sister group to all other flowering plants; diverged more than 130 million years ago; xylem lacks vessel elements; features of early flowering plants inferred by comparison

items.passage: Several analyses of the fossil record have concluded that dinosaurs were already in decline, with speciation failing to keep pace with extinction, for millions of years before an asteroid struck Earth 66 million years ago. But when paleontologist Joseph Bonsor and colleagues applied a different set of statistical models to twelve dinosaur phylogenies, they found little support for such a downturn; some groups, such as hadrosaurs and ceratopsians, were apparently thriving until the impact. The team attributes the conflicting conclusions to sampling biases in the fossil record and to differences in analytical methods.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
options: It discusses a study to argue that some groups of dinosaurs, such as hadrosaurs and ceratopsians, were thriving before the impact even though dinosaurs as a whole were in decline.
It discusses a study to suggest that differences in analytical methods, rather than biases in how the fossil record was sampled, explain why earlier analyses detected a decline in dinosaurs.
It presents research showing that the fossil record is too incomplete to reveal how dinosaur diversity changed over time.
It discusses a study to suggest that an apparent trend in the history of a group of animals may reflect how the evidence was gathered and analyzed.
items.explanation: The text opens with a conclusion some analyses have reached: dinosaurs were declining long before the asteroid impact. It then reports that Bonsor and colleagues, using different models, found little support for that decline, and that they trace the disagreement to biased fossil sampling and to differences in methods. So the text uses the study to suggest that the apparent decline may come from how the evidence was collected and analyzed, as choice D says.

A.recipe: first clause true, later clause reversed (REV)
A.why_wrong: The study did find hadrosaurs and ceratopsians apparently thriving, but it found little support for any overall decline; the thriving groups are offered as evidence against the decline, not as exceptions to it.

B.recipe: first clause true, half of the explanation dropped and set against the other (SWAP)
B.why_wrong: The team blames both sampling biases in the fossil record and differences in analytical methods; the text does not set one against the other or rule out the sampling biases.

C.why_wrong: The researchers blame sampling gaps for the earlier conclusion, but they still reach a conclusion of their own about dinosaur diversification, so the text does not claim the record reveals nothing.

sources.what: Bonsor, Barrett, Raven and Cooper (2020, Royal Society Open Science): twelve dinosaur phylogenies, no strong support for a downturn before the K-Pg boundary; disagreement attributed to sampling biases in the fossil record and differences in analytical methodology; hadrosaurs and ceratopsians thriving (Bath press release)

items.passage: In 1957 geochemist Katsuko Saruhashi became the first woman to earn a doctorate in science from the University of Tokyo. Working at a government meteorological laboratory, she developed new methods for detecting radioactive substances in seawater and used them to trace fallout from the nuclear weapons tests that the United States carried out in the Pacific in the 1950s. When American scientists doubted her measurements, she and oceanographer Theodore Folsom analyzed identical samples, and their results differed by less than 10 percent. Her findings, so confirmed, helped justify the eventual prohibition of above-ground nuclear testing.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
options: It introduces a scientist, describes a method she developed, and then explains why that method was later replaced by a more accurate one devised in the United States.
It notes a scientist’s early distinction, describes the research she carried out, and then explains how her results were verified and what effect they eventually had.
It mentions a scientist’s academic achievement, outlines the research she conducted on seawater, and then explains how she helped write an agreement banning certain weapons tests.

It identifies a milestone in a scientist’s education, summarizes her work on radioactive fallout, and then describes how a dispute over her measurements was settled in favor of the scientists who had doubted them.
items.explanation: The first sentence notes Saruhashi’s early distinction (the first woman to earn a science doctorate at the University of Tokyo). The second describes her research on radioactive fallout in seawater. The last two sentences explain how a side-by-side test with an American oceanographer confirmed her results and how those results helped justify banning above-ground nuclear tests. Choice B follows that order.

A.recipe: first moves right, last move reversed (REV)
A.why_wrong: The comparison with Folsom confirmed her results; the text never says her method was replaced by an American one.

C.recipe: first moves right, invented last move (INV)
C.why_wrong: The text says her confirmed findings helped justify the ban on above-ground testing; it never says she helped write any agreement.

D.recipe: first moves right, last move reversed (REV)
D.why_wrong: There was a dispute over her measurements, but the joint analysis confirmed them: the two labs’ results differed by less than 10 percent, and the text calls her findings “so confirmed.”

sources.what: Saruhashi: first woman to earn a PhD in science at the University of Tokyo (1957); new method for measuring radioactive fallout; joint analysis with Ted Folsom of identical samples, less than 10% discrepancy; research provided justification for prohibiting above-ground nuclear testing

items.passage:
The following text is from Susanna Moodie’s 1852 memoir Roughing It in the Bush. Moodie, a recent immigrant to Canada from England, had asked her neighbors to milk her cow because she did not know how; they laughed and refused.

After many ineffectual attempts, I succeeded at last, and bore my half-pail of milk in triumph to the house. Yes! I felt prouder of that milk than many an author of the best thing he ever wrote, whether in verse or prose; and it was doubly sweet when I considered that I had procured it without being under any obligation to my ill-natured neighbours. I had learned a useful lesson of independence, to which, in after-years, I had often again to refer.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
options: To describe the narrator’s efforts to persuade her neighbors to teach her how to milk a cow
To convey the narrator’s satisfaction at having managed a difficult task without help
To suggest that the narrator hopes to become an author by writing about her life on the farm
To show that the narrator regrets having quarreled with her neighbors
items.explanation: After “many ineffectual attempts,” the narrator finally milks the cow and carries the milk home “in triumph.” She says she felt prouder of the milk than an author of his best work, and that it was “doubly sweet” because she owed nothing to her unkind neighbors. The text conveys her satisfaction at doing something hard on her own, as choice B says.

A.why_wrong: The neighbors had already refused, and the narrator’s attempts were at milking, not at persuading anyone to teach her.

C.why_wrong: The author is a comparison for how proud she felt; the text says nothing about her wanting to write.

D.why_wrong: She calls the neighbors “ill-natured” and is glad to owe them nothing; she expresses no regret.

sources.what: Moodie, Roughing It in the Bush (1852), excerpt copied exactly

items.notes: Literature (memoir). Key B. Context line summarizes the preceding scene (the neighbors laugh and refuse); the excerpt itself is unchanged.

items.passage:
The following text is from Elizabeth Keckley’s 1868 memoir Behind the Scenes. Keckley, then enslaved in St. Louis, Missouri, needed $1,200 to buy freedom for herself and her son; a friend, Mrs. Le Bourgois, offered to raise it.

Mrs. Le Bourgois, God bless her dear good heart, was more than successful. The twelve hundred dollars were raised, and at last my son and myself were free. Free, free! what a glorious ring to the word. Free! the bitter heart-struggle was over. Free! the soul could go out to heaven and to God with no chains to clog its flight or pull it down. Free! the earth wore a brighter look, and the very stars seemed to sing with joy.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
options: To describe how Mrs. Le Bourgois persuaded others to contribute to the narrator’s cause
To express the narrator’s concern about how she will support her son now that they are free
To convey the narrator’s overwhelming joy at the end of her long struggle for freedom
To explain why the narrator chose to remain in St. Louis after she gained her freedom

It explains why farmers in Indonesia have started placing nets over their cacao trees.
It describes research that tested whether certain animals affect a crop and reports what the researchers found.
It argues that bats are more helpful to cacao farmers than birds are.
items.explanation: The text begins with an open question: how much do birds and bats affect cacao harvests? It then describes how Maas and colleagues kept the animals away from some trees with nets and found that yields dropped by about 31 percent. Choice C describes this: research testing the animals’ effect on a crop, and its result.

A.why_wrong: The study compared trees with and without nets on cacao plantations; it did not compare cacao farms with other farms.

B.why_wrong: The nets were part of the experiment, and the results suggest that keeping birds and bats away lowers yields, so the text gives no reason for farmers to use nets.

D.why_wrong: The text reports the effect of excluding birds and bats together and does not rank one above the other.

sources.what: Maas, Clough and Tscharntke (2013, Ecology Letters), Sulawesi: exclosures kept birds and bats from cacao trees by day, night or both; yields fell 31 percent when they were excluded

items.notes: Area: natural science (agricultural ecology). Key C. Mechanism given with a hedge ('probably because more of the insects that damage the crop survived').

items.passage: It has long been claimed that a culture’s instrumental music echoes the rhythms of its spoken language, but empirical evidence was lacking. To test the idea, Aniruddh Patel and Joseph Daniele borrowed a measure linguists use to quantify speech rhythm, the normalized pairwise variability index (nPVI), which captures the durational contrast between successive vowels. Spoken English, in which adjacent vowels frequently differ sharply in length, scores considerably higher on this index than spoken French. Applied instead to successive notes in instrumental themes by English and French composers, the index revealed an analogous difference.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
options: It discusses a study that adapted a tool from the analysis of speech in order to provide support for a long-standing but untested claim about music.
It describes a study that compared rhythm in the speech and music of two cultures and concluded that composers had deliberately imitated the sound of their own language.
It discusses a study that relied on the rhythms of instrumental music to explain why vowel durations vary more in spoken English than in spoken French.
It describes a study that applied a measure of speech rhythm to music in order to test whether linguists could rely on that measure when comparing languages.
items.explanation: The text opens with an old claim, that a culture’s music echoes the rhythm of its language, and notes that evidence for it was lacking. It then describes how Patel and Daniele took the nPVI, a measure linguists use for speech, applied it to musical themes, and found the same English–French difference in music as in speech. Choice A states this purpose: a tool borrowed from the study of speech was used to support a long-standing but untested idea about music.

B.why_wrong: The study did compare English and French speech and music, but it found a measured similarity in rhythm; the text says nothing about composers setting out to imitate their language.

C.why_wrong: The difference in vowel durations between English and French is the starting point, taken from linguistics; the study used it to examine music, not music to explain speech.

D.why_wrong: The study did carry a speech measure over to music, but it did so to test the old claim that music echoes speech; the text treats the measure as trusted and never asks whether linguists can rely on it.

sources.what: Patel and Daniele (2003, Cognition 87): the nPVI, a measure of speech rhythm, applied to English and French speech and to themes by English and French classical composers; English and French musical themes differ significantly on this measure, as their speech does; empirical support for the long-held claim that spoken prosody leaves an imprint on a culture’s music

items.notes: Area: social science and music (music cognition). Key A. Hard band 6: the key is paraphrased away from the passage (no nPVI, vowels, English or French in it) and needs two linked steps (the claim was untested; a speech measure was carried over to music). Each wrong option keeps a true element (English themes resemble English speech; the vowel-duration difference; the method) and fails on motive, direction or stance. replaced D (cast doubt on the method, a stance flip from the start) with a right-study, wrong-purpose option (testing whether linguists can rely on the measure)

items.passage:
The following text is from Thomas Love Peacock’s 1818 novel Nightmare Abbey. Scythrop, the only son of the melancholy Mr Glowry, often spends vacations at the London home of his uncle, Mr Hilary.

At the house of Mr Hilary, Scythrop first saw the beautiful Miss Emily Girouette. He fell in love; which is nothing new. He was favourably received; which is nothing strange. Mr Glowry and Mr Girouette had a meeting on the occasion, and quarrelled about the terms of the bargain; which is neither new nor strange. The lovers were torn asunder, weeping and vowing everlasting constancy; and, in three weeks after this tragical event, the lady was led a smiling bride to the altar, by the Honourable Mr Lackwit; which is neither strange nor new.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
options: It recounts a courtship and its sudden end while suggesting that the young man’s father was chiefly to blame for that end.
It relates a courtship and its sudden end while presenting every stage of it as commonplace and predictable.
It traces a courtship to its sudden end while dwelling on the lasting sorrow that the separation causes both lovers.
It follows a courtship to its sudden end while emphasizing how long the young woman hesitated before agreeing to marry another man.
items.explanation: The narrator follows the courtship step by step: Scythrop falls in love, is well received, the two fathers quarrel over the terms, and three weeks after the lovers part, the lady marries someone else. After each step the narrator adds a remark such as “which is nothing new” or “which is neither strange nor new.” These refrains present every stage, even the sudden ending, as ordinary and expected, as choice B says.

A.why_wrong: The courtship does end after a quarrel, but it is a quarrel between both fathers “about the terms of the bargain”; the text does not single out Mr Glowry or blame anyone.

C.recipe: first half true, word hook on “weeping” and “tragical” (LIT)
C.why_wrong: The lovers do part “weeping,” but three weeks later the young woman is “a smiling bride,” and the narrator calls even this “tragical event” nothing strange; the text does not dwell on any lasting sorrow.

D.why_wrong: The young woman marries “in three weeks after” the parting and goes to the altar “smiling”; the text presents her marriage as quick, not as the end of a long hesitation.

sources.what: Peacock, Nightmare Abbey (1818), chapter I, text copied exactly

items.notes: Literature (satirical novel, 1818). Key B. Band-7 moves: archaic, ironic narration; the key is abstract (no names, no events) and names the narrator's stance, inferred from the repeated refrain; after review every distractor opens with the true plot and fails on one later link. Context line follows chapter I (Scythrop passes vacations at his uncle's London house).

fixes: all distractors rebuilt to share the true first half (a courtship and its sudden end): A blames the young man’s father, C claims lasting sorrow (hooks “weeping”, “tragical”), D claims a long hesitation the “three weeks” rules out; C and D used to fail in their first clause

items.passage:
The following text is from Henry Mackenzie’s 1771 novel The Man of Feeling. Harley’s friends want him to travel to London to seek favors from influential people.

They did not fail to enumerate the many advantages which a certain degree of spirit and assurance gives a man who would make a figure in the world: they repeated their instances of good fortune in others, ascribed them all to a happy forwardness of disposition; and made so copious a recital of the disadvantages which attend the opposite weakness, that a stranger, who had heard them, would have been led to imagine, that in the British code there was some disqualifying statute against any citizen who should be convicted of—modesty.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
options: It conveys how insistently Harley’s friends urged boldness on him, noting that they pointed to a British law that penalized modest citizens.
It shows how hard Harley’s friends pressed him to be bolder and explains why he finally agreed to follow their advice.
It conveys how insistently Harley’s friends urged boldness on him, using an ironic exaggeration to show how far they carried their argument.
It describes the friends’ insistence that Harley be bolder while revealing that they privately envied the success his modesty had brought him.
items.explanation: Harley’s friends list the advantages of “spirit and assurance,” credit other people’s good fortune to “forwardness,” and dwell so heavily on the drawbacks of “the opposite weakness” that a listener might imagine British law punished people for being modest. That imagined law is an exaggeration that shows how hard the friends pressed the case that Harley’s modesty was a handicap. Choice C states this purpose.

A.recipe: first half true, figure read literally (LIT)
A.why_wrong: The friends did praise boldness, but the “disqualifying statute” is only what a stranger “would have been led to imagine” from their talk; no real law is described, and the friends never cite one.

B.why_wrong: The friends did press Harley hard, but the text ends with their arguments; it never reports Harley’s response or explains any decision of his.

D.why_wrong: The friends did urge boldness, but they credit good fortune to “forwardness,” not modesty; nothing suggests Harley’s modesty had brought him success or that his friends envied him.

sources.what: Mackenzie, The Man of Feeling (1771): Harley's friends press him to accept Mr. Walton's offer of an introduction in London; paragraph on “spirit and assurance” and “modesty” copied exactly

items.notes: Literature (novel, 1771). Key C. items.passage: Literary critic Ian Watt coined the term “delayed decoding” for a narrative technique he identified throughout Joseph Conrad’s fiction: a narrator conveys a sensory impression as it is initially experienced and only subsequently supplies its cause. In Heart of Darkness, for instance, <u>Marlow, piloting a steamboat along an African river, observes little sticks flying around him; only moments later does he recognize them as arrows and realize that the vessel is under attack</u>. By postponing the explanation, Watt suggested, Conrad situates readers alongside a character who has not yet interpreted what he perceives.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined portion in the text as a whole?
options: It summarizes a scene that Watt regarded as an exception to the narrative method he otherwise found throughout Conrad’s fiction.
It recounts the episode from Heart of Darkness that, according to the text, first led Watt to propose the term “delayed decoding” for this technique.
It recounts an episode from Heart of Darkness that, as the following sentence suggests, Watt cited to show a weakness in Conrad’s storytelling.
It provides an instance of the technique named in the previous sentence, a technique whose effect the following sentence explains.
items.explanation: The first sentence defines delayed decoding: the narrator reports a sensation first and its cause only later. The underlined portion, introduced with “for instance,” describes Marlow seeing little sticks and only later realizing they are arrows, which is exactly that pattern. The last sentence then explains what the technique does for readers. Choice D captures both links.

A.why_wrong: The portion does summarize a scene, but “for instance” presents the scene as an example of the technique, not an exception to it.

B.why_wrong: The text gives the arrows scene as one instance of the technique; it never says this scene is what led Watt to coin the term.

C.why_wrong: The portion is an episode from the novel, but the following sentence explains what the technique does for readers (it places them beside a character who has not yet understood what he sees); it points to no weakness.

sources.what: Ian Watt's “delayed decoding” in Conrad, discussed through the “little sticks” and “arrows” passage of Heart of Darkness (review of Johan Warodell, Conrad's Decentered Fiction, 2022)

items.notes: Area: humanities (literary criticism). Key D. Hard band 6: two-part key (instance of the technique named before; its effect described after); A, B and C open with a true description of the span and fail in the second clause (exception, origin, weakness). Watt coined the term in Conrad in the Nineteenth Century (1979); the scene is Marlow's attack on the river (“Sticks, little sticks, were flying about”), paraphrased. Watt's view of the effect is given with “suggested,” not quoted.

fixes: replaced C (an interpretation of Marlow’s character, false from its first clause) with a true-first-clause option that fails on “a weakness in Conrad’s storytelling”
checks: core claim (Watt’s delayed decoding, the sticks and arrows scene) confirmed in the cited Conrad Society review

items.passage: Allensworth, California, was established in 1908 by Allen Allensworth, a retired army chaplain who had been born into slavery, and several other Black investors, who envisioned an autonomous agricultural community where Black families could acquire and cultivate land. The settlement expanded rapidly; by 1914 it possessed a church, a library, and a school, and it had organized California’s first school district administered by African Americans. That same year, however, the railroad relocated its station to a neighboring town, and much of the water the settlers depended on for irrigation was diverted; as harvests failed, many residents departed.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
options: To describe the founding and early growth of a town and show how its founder’s military career shaped the way it was governed
To describe the founding and early growth of a town and identify setbacks that contributed to its decline
To recount how a town was founded and grew, and to argue that state officials could have prevented its decline
To trace the history of a town from its founding to its eventual preservation as a historic site
items.explanation: The first sentence describes who founded Allensworth and why. The second describes its quick growth: a church, a library, a school, and California’s first school district run by African Americans. The last sentence turns with “however” to the setbacks, the loss of the railroad stop and the diversion of water, that led residents to leave. Choice B covers all three parts.

A.why_wrong: The text does describe the founding and growth and mentions that Allensworth had been an army chaplain, but it never connects his military career to how the town was governed.

C.why_wrong: The text does recount the founding and growth and reports that water was diverted, but it makes no argument about what could have saved the town and mentions no state officials.

D.why_wrong: The text ends with residents leaving after 1914; it says nothing about the town later becoming a historic site.

items.passage: There Is No Other, a 2019 album by American vocalist Rhiannon Giddens and Italian jazz musician Francesco Turrisi, interprets songs drawn from European and American musical traditions. Rather than recruiting an ensemble, the two musicians performed most of the material themselves, alternating among instruments that include the banjo and the frame drum. Writer John Jeremiah Sullivan has contended that the album effectively substantiates musicologist Peter van der Merwe’s thesis that West African and Irish musical traditions, both influenced centuries earlier by the Islamic world, were already closely related when they converged in the American South.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
options: It introduces a collaborative album, describes how the music on it was performed, and then presents one writer’s complaint that the album has been largely overlooked.
It introduces an album by two musicians, explains how they performed its songs, and then reports a writer’s doubt that two players alone could do justice to such varied traditions.
It introduces a collaborative album, describes how the music on it was performed, and then presents one writer’s view of what the album demonstrates.
It introduces an album, describes the instruments its two makers played, and then reports a writer’s view that the album supports a theory the two musicians had themselves proposed.
items.explanation: The first sentence introduces the album and the two musicians who made it. The second describes their approach: they played most of the music themselves on several instruments instead of using a band. The third reports Sullivan’s view that the album supports van der Merwe’s claim about the shared roots of West African and Irish music. Choice C names these three moves in order.

A.recipe: first two moves true, third move invented (INV)
A.why_wrong: The first two moves fit, but the writer the text cites treats the album as evidence for a thesis; nothing says it has been overlooked.

B.recipe: first two moves true, third move stance flipped (STANCE)
B.why_wrong: The first two moves fit, and the pair did play most of the music themselves, but Sullivan says the album substantiates a thesis; he raises no doubt about the performance.

D.recipe: first two moves true, theory misattributed (SWAP)
D.why_wrong: The first two moves fit, and Sullivan does say the album supports a theory, but it is musicologist Peter van der Merwe’s thesis, not one the performers proposed.

items.passage: Giant and colossal squid possess eyes up to approximately 27 centimeters in diameter, the largest of any animal. Body size cannot explain this: swordfish, of comparable mass, have eyes only about 9 centimeters wide. Nor can the demands of locating prey in the dimly lit deep ocean, since, as Dan-Eric Nilsson and colleagues calculated, eyes exceeding a swordfish’s offer negligible improvement in detecting the small targets most deep-sea animals pursue. Instead, the researchers persuasively argue, such eyes enable squid to detect approaching sperm whales by the bioluminescence of the minute organisms the whales disturb, up to 120 meters away.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
options: It describes an unusual feature of an animal, explains why two proposed causes of that feature are inadequate, and then argues that its true cause may never be determined.
It introduces a striking feature of an animal, explains why two possible accounts of it fall short, and then presents two further accounts that the author considers equally likely.
It describes an unusual feature of an animal, explains why two proposed accounts of that feature are inadequate, and then reports observations of living squid that confirmed a third account.
It introduces a remarkable feature of an animal, explains why two possible accounts of that feature fall short, and then presents an alternative account that the author endorses.
items.explanation: The text first introduces the giant squid’s enormous eyes. It then rejects two possible explanations: body size (swordfish of similar size have much smaller eyes) and finding prey (eyes that large add little to seeing small targets). Finally it presents Nilsson and colleagues’ explanation, spotting approaching sperm whales by the glow they stir up, and calls their argument persuasive. Choice D describes these three moves.

A.recipe: first two moves true, third move reversed (STANCE)
A.why_wrong: The text does rule out two causes, but it then offers a third explanation and calls it persuasive; it never suggests the cause may never be known.

B.recipe: first two moves true, third move miscounted (REL)
B.why_wrong: The text does rule out two accounts, but it then presents a single alternative, which the author calls persuasive, not two accounts held to be equally likely.

C.recipe: first two moves true, third move’s outcome invented (INV)
C.why_wrong: The text does rule out two accounts, but the third rests on the researchers’ calculations and argument; the text reports no observations of living squid confirming it.

sources.what: Nilsson, Johnsen and colleagues (2012, Current Biology): giant and colossal squid eyes far larger than those of a similar-sized swordfish (about 3 inches); extra eye size matters little for the small-object tasks of most deep-sea animals but lets the squid detect the bioluminescence a sperm whale stirs up at about 120 meters

The following text is from Elizabeth Stoddard’s 1863 short story “Lemorne Versus Huell.” The narrator, Margaret, has come to accompany her wealthy aunt, Eliza Huell, on a two-month stay at the seaside.

At the beginning of each visit to Aunt Eliza I was in the habit of dwelling on the contrast between her way of living and ours. We lived from “hand to mouth.” Every thing about her wore a hereditary air; for she lived in my grandfather’s house, and it was the same as in his day. If I was at home when these contrasts occurred to me I should have felt angry; as it was, I felt them as in a dream—the china, the silver, the old furniture, and the excellent fare soothed me.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
options: To convey the narrator’s response to the differences between her aunt’s circumstances and her own family’s
To explain how the narrator’s family came to lose the wealth that her aunt still enjoys
To show that the narrator resents her aunt for living in comfort while the narrator’s own family struggles to get by
To emphasize the narrator’s admiration for the changes her aunt has made to her grandfather’s house
items.explanation: The narrator says that on each visit she thinks about the contrast between her aunt’s way of living and her own family’s, since her family lives “from hand to mouth” while her aunt lives in the grandfather’s unchanged house. She adds that at home such thoughts would make her angry, but at her aunt’s the china, silver, and good food soothe her. The text is about her reaction to these differences, as choice A says.

B.why_wrong: The text contrasts the two households but never explains how the narrator’s family came to have less money.

C.why_wrong: The narrator says she would feel angry only if she thought of the contrast at home; at her aunt’s house she feels soothed, and she never blames her aunt.

D.why_wrong: The narrator says the house is “the same as in his day,” so her aunt has not changed it.

sources.what: Elizabeth Stoddard, “Lemorne Versus Huell” (Harper's, 1863), text copied exactly

items.notes: Literature (short story, 1863). Key A. Medium: the key needs the whole paragraph (the contrast and the mixed feeling); C is the partial trap built on “I should have felt angry.” “Every thing” is Stoddard's spelling.

The following text is from Frances Trollope’s 1832 travel book Domestic Manners of the Americans. After a lengthy transatlantic voyage, Trollope and her family are approaching the mouth of the Mississippi River, which flows into the Gulf of Mexico.

The shores of this river are so utterly flat, that no object upon them is perceptible at sea, and we gazed with pleasure on the muddy ocean that met us, for it told us we were arrived, and seven weeks of sailing had wearied us; yet it was not without a feeling like regret that we passed from the bright blue waves, whose varying aspect had so long furnished our chief amusement, into the murky stream which now received us.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
options: To explain why the narrator found the river more appealing than the open sea
To convey the narrator’s mixed feelings as a long sea voyage comes to an end

items.passage: Many flowers reward their pollinators with nectar, but the South African plant Ceropegia sandersonii offers its visitors nothing at all; its principal pollinators are tiny Desmometopa flies, which ordinarily feed on the bodies of honeybees captured by spiders. Biologist Annemarie Heiduk and her colleagues discovered that the plant exploits this feeding habit: <u>its flowers emit a scent closely resembling the chemicals that honeybees release when they are attacked</u>. Lured by the scent, the flies crawl into the flowers, which temporarily trap them, and they pick up pollen before escaping.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined portion in the text as a whole?
options: It explains how the plant attracts the insects that pollinate it.
It identifies the reason that the flies feed on honeybees.
It describes how spiders locate the honeybees they capture.
It contrasts the plant’s scent with the scents of flowers that offer nectar.
items.explanation: The text says the plant offers its pollinators no reward and that the flies normally feed on honeybees caught by spiders. The underlined portion explains how the plant takes advantage of this: its scent imitates the chemicals released by honeybees under attack, which draws the flies in. So the portion explains how the plant attracts its pollinators.

B.why_wrong: The text says the flies feed on honeybees caught by spiders, but the underlined portion is about the flower’s scent, not why the flies eat honeybees.

D.why_wrong: The text mentions nectar-producing flowers in its first sentence, but the underlined portion describes this plant’s scent without comparing it with theirs.

items.passage: Because large whales spend most of their lives submerged and are difficult to approach safely, monitoring their health presents considerable challenges. It presents an unexpected finding about the bacteria in whales’ airways.
It identifies a problem with earlier methods of studying large whales.
It describes how the researchers obtained the samples they analyzed.

B.why_wrong: The finding about a shared core community of bacteria comes in the following sentence; the underlined sentence describes how samples were collected.

items.passage: Why does the reflective layer at the back of a reindeer’s eye change color with the seasons? Like many mammals, reindeer possess a tapetum lucidum, a mirrorlike tissue behind the retina; in Arctic reindeer, however, this tissue is golden in summer but deep blue in winter. Researchers Karl-Arne Stokkan, Glen Jeffery, and colleagues propose an explanation: during the prolonged winter darkness, permanently dilated pupils probably increase pressure inside the eye, compressing the tissue’s collagen fibers so that it reflects shorter, bluer wavelengths. Instead of returning light directly out of the eye, the blue tissue scatters more of it through the retina, enhancing sensitivity at some cost to visual sharpness.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
options: The text asks why a trait of an animal changes over the year, then explains why researchers have been unable to answer that question.
The text asks why a trait of an animal changes over the year, then presents an explanation that a team of researchers has proposed.
The text describes a trait that many mammals share, then argues that reindeer are the only mammals that lack it.
The text compares the eyes of two kinds of animals, then describes how those animals find food in the dark.
items.explanation: The text opens with a question about why the reflective layer in a reindeer’s eye changes color with the seasons. The rest of the text gives the explanation that Stokkan, Jeffery, and colleagues propose: in winter, pressure inside the eye compresses the tissue so that it reflects bluer light and scatters more light through the retina, making the eye more sensitive in the dark. Choice B describes this question-then-answer structure.

A.recipe: first move right, later move reversed (REV)
A.why_wrong: The text does ask why the trait changes, but it then presents the researchers’ proposed answer rather than saying they could not find one.

C.recipe: first move partly right, later move reversed (REV)
C.why_wrong: The text says reindeer, like many mammals, have a tapetum lucidum; it never claims they lack it.

D.why_wrong: The text discusses only reindeer and says nothing about how they find food.

B): reindeer tapetum lucidum golden in summer, deep blue in winter; raised intraocular pressure probably from permanent pupil dilation compresses collagen; blue reflection scatters light through photoreceptors, increasing sensitivity at the cost of acuity

items.notes: Area: natural science (vision). Key B. 'Probably' kept from the paper's hedge on the cause of the pressure.

items.passage: William Henry Fox Talbot’s The Pencil of Nature (1844), the first commercially published book illustrated with photographs, is celebrated as a milestone in the history of photography. But eight months before Talbot’s book appeared, botanist Anna Atkins had begun issuing Photographs of British Algae, a book of cyanotype prints of dried seaweed. Atkins’s privately published volume came first, and she deserves to be remembered as a pioneer of the photographic book.

options: To explain how Talbot developed the printing process that Atkins later used to make the images in her book
To compare the quality of the images in two early books of photographs
To argue that Atkins deserves recognition for a book that came before a more celebrated one
To describe the kinds of seaweed that Atkins collected along the coast of Britain
items.explanation: The text notes that Talbot’s 1844 book is celebrated as a milestone, then points out that Atkins began issuing her book of cyanotypes eight months earlier and concludes that she “deserves to be remembered as a pioneer.” The text therefore argues that Atkins should be recognized for a book that preceded Talbot’s better-known one.

There was no escape; and at last his hour was hard upon him. Therefore he brooded on the fence and gazed with envy at his wistful Duke.

items.passage: In Pedagogy of the Oppressed (1968), Brazilian educator Paulo Freire criticized what he called the “banking” model of education, in which teachers deposit knowledge into passive students as if filling empty containers; instead, he argued, learners should help create knowledge through dialogue. Freire’s ideas shaped the work of his fellow Brazilian Augusto Boal, who in the 1970s developed what he called the Theatre of the Oppressed. In Forum Theatre, one of its best-known forms, audience members may stop a short scene depicting an injustice and step onstage to act out their own solutions, becoming what Boal called “spect-actors.”
items.stem: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?

The text outlines an educator’s view of how people learn best, then describes a form of theater shaped by that view.
The text outlines an educator’s view of how people learn best, then explains why theater artists later rejected that view.
The text traces the history of theater in Brazil, then lists the techniques that its directors most often use.
items.explanation: The first sentence presents Freire’s view that learners should help create knowledge through dialogue rather than passively receive it. The rest of the text describes Boal’s Theatre of the Oppressed, which Freire’s ideas shaped and in which audience members step onstage to act out solutions. Choice B describes this idea-then-influenced-work structure.

C.recipe: first move right, later move reversed (REV)

D.why_wrong: The text discusses one theater practice influenced by one educator, not the history of Brazilian theater or its directors’ usual techniques.

The following text is from Lord Byron’s 1809 poem English Bards and Scotch Reviewers. Fitzgerald was a minor poet of the time.

Still must I hear?—shall hoarse Fitzgerald bawl
His creaking couplets in a tavern hall,
And I not sing, lest, haply [perhaps], Scotch Reviews [Scottish literary journals]
Should dub me scribbler, and denounce my Muse?
Prepare for rhyme—I’ll publish, right or wrong:
Fools are my theme, let Satire be my song.
Oh! Nature’s noblest gift—my grey goose-quill!
Slave of my thoughts, obedient to my will,
Torn from thy parent bird to form a pen,
That mighty instrument of little men!
items.stem: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
options: The speaker complains that audiences prefer another poet’s work to his own, then resolves to imitate that poet’s popular style.
The speaker admits that critics were right to call him a scribbler, then promises to write more carefully in the future.
The speaker refuses to let the threat of harsh reviews keep him silent, then declares the kind of poetry he means to write.
The speaker recalls how he first learned to write poetry, then thanks the friend who gave him his first pen.
items.explanation: The speaker first asks whether he must stay silent, out of fear that Scottish reviewers will call him a scribbler, while a poor poet like Fitzgerald keeps performing. He answers by announcing, “I’ll publish, right or wrong,” names satire of fools as his theme, and calls on his pen for the task. Choice C gives both moves.

A.why_wrong: The speaker mocks Fitzgerald’s “creaking couplets”; he says nothing about audiences preferring Fitzgerald and has no wish to imitate him.

B.why_wrong: The speaker does not concede that the reviewers are right; he refuses to be silenced by them and will publish “right or wrong.”

D.why_wrong: The goose-quill is the pen he will write with, praised as “Nature’s noblest gift”; the poem mentions no lessons and no friend who gave him a pen.

items.passage: Tawny crazy ants (Nylanderia fulva), which reached the southern United States from South America, frequently displace imported fire ants (Solenopsis invicta), another South American invader notorious for its venomous sting. Investigating this displacement, Edward LeBrun, Nathan Jones, and Lawrence Gilbert observed that after exposure to fire ant venom, a crazy ant applies secretions from an abdominal gland to its exoskeleton. Laboratory bioassays demonstrated that formic acid in these secretions detoxifies the venom, a capability that, the researchers propose, probably contributes substantially to the crazy ants’ competitive success.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
options: It describes a chemical defense used by one invasive ant species in order to argue that the species should be controlled before it spreads any farther.
It summarizes research that identifies a defensive behavior in one invasive ant species and suggests how it may help that species prevail over another.
It reports how one invasive ant protects itself from a rival’s venom in order to show that the venom is less dangerous to other insects than scientists had believed.
It summarizes research identifying a chemical made by one invasive ant species and explaining how that chemical allows the species to locate its rivals’ nests.
items.explanation: The text first notes that tawny crazy ants often displace fire ants, then describes what LeBrun and his colleagues observed (crazy ants smear a gland secretion over themselves after exposure to fire ant venom), then reports that formic acid in the secretion detoxifies the venom, which the researchers think probably helps explain the crazy ants’ success. Choice B states both parts of this purpose: the research identifies a defensive behavior and suggests how it may help one invader prevail over another.

A.why_wrong: The text does describe a chemical defense in an invasive ant, but it only reports the research; it never recommends controlling the species or warns about its spread.

C.why_wrong: The text does describe a crazy ant protecting itself from fire ant venom, but it says nothing about the venom’s effect on other insects or about what scientists had believed; the detox behavior is presented as the crazy ant’s own competitive advantage.

D.recipe: first part true, later link invented (INV)
D.why_wrong: The research does identify a chemical the crazy ants make (formic acid), but the text says it detoxifies fire ant venom, not that it helps the ants find their rivals’ nests.

items.passage:
The following text is from Clarissa Scott Delany’s 1926 poem “The Mask.”

So detached and cool she is
No motion e’er betrays
The secret life within her soul,
The anguish of her days.

She seems to look upon the world
With cold ironic eyes,
To spurn emotion’s fevered sway,
To scoff at tears and sighs.

But once a woman with a child
Passed by her on the street,
And once she heard from casual lips
A man’s name, bitter-sweet.

Such baffled yearning in her eyes,
Such pain upon her face!
I turned aside until the mask
Was slipped once more in place.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
options: To suggest that the woman’s outward coldness is a reaction to the speaker’s close observation of her
To reveal that the woman’s coldness is a pretense, one she gives up once she decides to confide in the speaker
To contrast the woman’s indifference toward strangers with her devotion to her own child and husband
To portray a woman whose composure hides a private sorrow that chance reminders briefly expose
items.explanation: The first two stanzas describe a woman who seems “detached and cool,” with “cold ironic eyes,” while “no motion” betrays “the anguish of her days.” The last two stanzas describe two chance moments, seeing a woman with a child and hearing a man’s name, that bring “baffled yearning” and “pain” to her face until her composure returns. The poem’s purpose is to portray a woman whose calm hides a private sorrow that such reminders briefly reveal, as choice D says.

A.why_wrong: The woman does appear cold, but the poem never links this to the speaker; the speaker only turns aside, out of tact, when her pain shows.

B.recipe: first part true, later link invented (INV)
B.why_wrong: Her coldness is indeed a pretense (the “mask”), but she never confides in the speaker: the speaker turns aside, and the mask is “slipped once more in place.”

C.why_wrong: She does seem indifferent, but the woman with a child is a stranger who passes by, and the man’s name is heard from “casual lips”; the poem mentions no child or husband of her own.

“The Mask” first published in Palms, 1926

items.passage: From 1943 to 1947, the Council on Books in Wartime, an organization of American publishers, distributed free paperbacks to US service members overseas. Printed inexpensively on digest-magazine presses and sized to fit in a uniform pocket, the books reached soldiers in hospitals, aboard troopships, and at remote outposts supplied by airdrop; <u>just before the 1944 invasion of Normandy, every soldier boarding a transport in southern England was handed one</u>. Historians of publishing credit the program with demonstrating that inexpensive paperbacks could attract an enormous readership, partly because it transformed so many young servicemen into habitual readers.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined portion in the text as a whole?
options: It gives a vivid instance of how thoroughly the books reached soldiers, which lends weight to the account of the program’s influence in the final sentence.
It offers a memorable example of the program’s reach, one that the text suggests persuaded military officials to keep distributing the books after the war ended.
It describes a moment when soldiers received the books, which the text presents as evidence that the titles were chosen mainly to prepare troops for combat.
It mentions a well-known military operation in order to show that the books were valued most by soldiers who were about to go into battle.
items.explanation: The second sentence lists the places the books reached, and the underlined portion caps the list with a striking case: every soldier boarding a transport before the Normandy invasion was handed a book. The final sentence says historians credit the program with proving that cheap paperbacks could find a vast audience, partly because it made readers of “so many young servicemen.” The underlined portion therefore illustrates the program’s reach, which supports that account of its influence, as choice A says.

B.recipe: first part true, later link invented (INV)
B.why_wrong: The portion does show the program’s reach, and distribution did run to 1947, but the text never says this example, or anything else, persuaded officials to continue the program.

C.why_wrong: The portion does describe soldiers receiving books, but the text says nothing about how titles were chosen or about preparing troops for combat.

D.why_wrong: The portion does mention the Normandy invasion, but the text never ranks which soldiers valued the books most; it uses the handout to show how widely the books reached soldiers, which supports the final sentence.

items.passage: In 1942, as Japanese Americans on the West Coast were being forcibly removed to incarceration camps, sculptor Isamu Noguchi, a New York resident exempt from the order, voluntarily entered the camp at Poston, Arizona, intending to make conditions there more humane. He drafted plans for the camp: <u>his blueprints designated space not only for an arts center, botanical gardens, and a cemetery but even for a zoo and a miniature golf course</u>. Within months, however, having received no support from camp administrators and feeling increasingly isolated, Noguchi was requesting his release; none of his designs was ever constructed.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined portion in the text as a whole?
options: It conveys how far-reaching Noguchi’s plans for the camp were, a scope that, according to the text, persuaded officials to grant his request to leave.
It lists facilities that Noguchi designed for the camp, which the text indicates were later built in simpler form by the people incarcerated there.

The final sentence then turns: officials gave no support, he soon sought release, and none of the designs was built. The underlined portion conveys the scale of his hopes, which heightens the contrast with that outcome, as choice C says.

B.why_wrong: The portion does list facilities Noguchi designed, but the final sentence says none of his designs was ever built, in any form.

items.passage: Dogs’ proficiency at following human pointing gestures has frequently been cited as evidence that domestication endowed dogs with a distinctive sensitivity to human communication, but that conclusion may be premature. In a 2008 study, Monique Udell, Nicole Dorey, and Clive Wynne tested wolves that had been hand-reared by people and socialized with them daily. Without any training, the wolves used a momentary pointing gesture by a distant experimenter to locate concealed food, whereas dogs living in a shelter, as well as pet dogs tested outdoors, generally failed to do so.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
options: It describes research comparing wolves and dogs in order to establish that wolves are generally more skilled than dogs at interpreting human communication.
It presents the study by Udell, Dorey, and Wynne to explain how dogs gradually acquired their skill at following human gestures during domestication.
It describes a 2008 study in order to criticize the methods that earlier researchers had used to test dogs’ responses to human pointing.
It discusses a study of wolves raised by people to suggest that an ability often credited to domestication might not depend on it.
items.explanation: The text opens with a common claim, that dogs’ skill at following pointing shows domestication gave them a special sensitivity, and warns that this conclusion “may be premature.” It then describes a study in which wolves raised by people followed a pointing gesture to food without training, while shelter dogs and pet dogs tested outdoors generally did not. The study is presented to suggest that the ability may not depend on domestication, as choice D says.

A.why_wrong: The text does compare wolves with some dogs, but it uses the result to caution about a claim concerning domestication; it does not try to show that wolves are generally better at reading people than dogs are.

B.why_wrong: The text does present this study, but the study suggests the ability need not come from domestication; it does not trace how dogs acquired it.

C.why_wrong: The text does describe a 2008 study, but it questions a conclusion drawn from dogs’ behavior, not the methods of earlier experiments, which it never describes.

sources.what: Udell, Dorey, Wynne (Animal Behaviour 2008), abstract: hand-reared, well-socialized wolves followed momentary distal human points to food without training; shelter dogs and dogs tested outdoors did not, pet dogs tested indoors did; domestication is not required for human-like social cognition in canids

items.passage: In the 1960s, folklorist Alan Lomax and collaborators at Columbia University launched Cantometrics, an ambitious project that sought to correlate the singing styles of the world’s cultures with their patterns of social organization. Rather than transcribing melodies, the team rated approximately 4,000 recorded songs from roughly 400 societies on 37 characteristics, including the degree of tension in singers’ voices and the extent to which members of a group blended together. Some musicologists, however, doubted that any quantity of such ratings could establish reliable connections between a community’s music and its social structure.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
options: It introduces a project linking music to society, describes the procedure used to analyze songs, and then conveys some scholars’ doubts about what that procedure could show.
It presents a project that compared music across cultures, explains why its researchers preferred rating recordings to transcribing them, and then notes an objection to that preference.
It introduces a cross-cultural study of singing, details how the songs were assessed, and then describes how the study’s methods were revised in response to its critics.
It describes the goal of a large research project, outlines the procedure its team followed, and then reports a result that the team regarded as confirming that goal.
items.explanation: The first sentence introduces Cantometrics and its aim of relating singing styles to how cultures are organized. The second describes the team’s procedure: rating some 4,000 songs on 37 features. items.passage: Copepods of the genus Calanus, minute crustaceans abundant in northern seas, ascend toward the surface at dusk and descend into deeper water at dawn, a schedule that allows them to graze on surface phytoplankton under cover of darkness while remaining invisible during daylight to fish, which are visual predators. Numerous other zooplankton follow the same daily schedule. In Dabob Bay, Washington, however, Mark Ohman and colleagues discovered that the copepod Pseudocalanus does the reverse, ascending by day and descending at night, apparently to avoid invertebrate predators that themselves migrate upward after dark.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
options: It accounts for a daily pattern of movement in one group of animals, observes that the pattern is common, and then describes a population whose contrary habit has yet to be explained.
It describes a daily movement and the reason for it, indicates that many organisms share it, and then reports evidence that the movement is less widespread than once assumed.
It explains why one kind of animal moves as it does each day, notes that this movement is widespread, and then presents a population that moves the opposite way for a comparable reason.
It identifies a daily pattern and its cause, states that the pattern is typical of similar organisms, and then explains how one population changed its pattern after a new predator appeared.

The second says many other zooplankton do the same. The third presents Pseudocalanus in Dabob Bay, which does the reverse, apparently to avoid predators that rise at night, so it too is avoiding predators. Choice C follows these moves, including the fact that the exception has a comparable explanation.

B.why_wrong: The text presents one population that does the opposite; it never suggests that the usual movement is less common than researchers thought.

D.recipe: moves 1 and 2 right, move 3 invented change over time (INV)
D.why_wrong: The text describes Pseudocalanus’s reverse migration and its likely reason, but says nothing about a change in its behavior or the arrival of a new predator.

The following text is adapted from Mór Jókai’s 1865 novel Debts of Honor (translated by Arthur B. Yolland in 1900). The narrator, a boy of ten, is being sent to live with a family in Pressburg in exchange for their daughter.

The journey to Pressburg lasted from early morning till late evening; only as twilight came on did a new thought begin to keep me awake: “What kind of a child could it be, for whom I was now being exchanged? Who was to usurp my place at table, in my bed-room, and in my mother’s heart? was she as much afraid of me as I was of her?”

For I was very much afraid of her.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
options: To describe the sights that the narrator notices during a long journey to a new town
To convey the narrator’s growing fear of the girl who will replace him at home
To explain why the narrator’s parents decided to send him away to Pressburg
To show the narrator’s eagerness to meet a girl who will become like a sister to him
items.explanation: As twilight falls on the journey, the narrator begins to wonder about the child “for whom I was now being exchanged”: who will “usurp my place at table, in my bed-room, and in my mother’s heart,” what she will be like, and whether she fears him as he fears her. He ends, “I was very much afraid of her.” The text conveys his growing fear of the girl who will replace him at home, as choice B says.

A.why_wrong: The journey is only the setting; the narrator describes no sights, only the questions that keep him awake.

C.why_wrong: The text never says why the exchange is being made; it focuses on the narrator’s thoughts about the girl.

The following text is adapted from Emilia Pardo Bazán’s 1885 novel The Swan of Vilamorta (translated by Mary J. Serrano in 1891). Segundo García is a young man from Vilamorta, a town in Galicia, Spain.

Segundo composed his first verses, cynical and pessimistic in intention, ingenuous in reality, before he had reached the age of seventeen. His classmates applauded him to the echo. He acquired in their eyes a certain prestige. Thenceforth he acquired the right to indulge in solitary walks, to laugh rarely, to surround his adventures with mystery, and not to play or take a drink for good-fellowship’s sake except when he felt in the humor.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
options: To portray how early praise from his classmates led a young poet to cultivate an air of mystery
To explain why Segundo’s classmates came to resent the attention and prestige that his first poems brought him
To show that Segundo’s first poems were admired by readers and critics throughout Spain
To suggest that Segundo later came to regret the gloomy and cynical tone of the poems he wrote as a youth
items.explanation: The text says Segundo wrote his first verses before seventeen, that his classmates “applauded him to the echo,” and that he gained “a certain prestige” in their eyes. With that prestige he “acquired the right” to take solitary walks, laugh rarely, and surround himself with mystery. The text thus portrays how early praise from his classmates led him to cultivate an aloof, mysterious manner, as choice A says.

items.passage: Packrats, rodents inhabiting the deserts of western North America, construct their dens from twigs, leaves, seeds, and other material collected within a short distance of home. It explains why packrats prefer to build their middens in especially dry places.
It describes a technique that researchers use to date the remains found in middens.
It explains how the plant material in packrat middens comes to be preserved.
items.explanation: The sentence before the underlined portion says middens would ordinarily decay. The underlined portion explains why they do not: the rats’ urine crystallizes into amberat, which cements the debris and slows its decay. The last sentence then explains why that matters to researchers. The portion describes how the plant material in middens is preserved, as choice D says.

A.why_wrong: The text says only that packrats gather material near their dens; the underlined portion is about what happens to the pile afterward, not how plants are chosen.

B.why_wrong: The portion mentions dry air as a condition for the urine to crystallize, but it says nothing about where packrats prefer to build.

C.why_wrong: Dating the remains is mentioned in the last sentence as something researchers do; the underlined portion describes a natural process caused by the rats.
